# Diagnosing Brake Pedal Sponginess in GM V6 Applications

A sudden transition from perfect braking performance to a pedal that sinks to the floor without engine power is a classic diagnostic puzzle, particularly in older GM vehicles like the 2000 Blazer with the 4.3L V6. The fact that the brakes feel firm when the ignition is off but go soft immediately upon starting the engine points directly to an issue within the vacuum assist system or its control logic, rather than a mechanical failure of the hydraulic components themselves.

The brake booster relies on engine manifold vacuum to amplify pedal pressure. When you press the pedal with the engine running, the booster uses this vacuum difference to push against the master cylinder diaphragm, effectively multiplying your foot force by roughly three times. If the booster loses its seal or cannot maintain that differential, you lose that mechanical advantage. This explains why the pedal travels further (less force multiplication) and requires significantly harder pushing to achieve the same deceleration, often leading to tire lockup before full stop capability is reached.

Since the master cylinder was replaced recently with no improvement, the focus must shift away from hydraulic leaks or internal piston wear in the new unit. If there were a hard leak in the wheel cylinders or calipers, the pedal would likely drop gradually over time as fluid escapes into a void, not just upon engine start. The immediate correlation with ignition status confirms the vacuum supply is compromised once the system pressurizes or changes state.

A critical, often overlooked component in this specific scenario is the brake booster check valve. This one-way valve prevents exhaust pressure from entering the booster while the engine runs and ensures that residual vacuum remains when the engine stops. If this internal spring-and-valve mechanism sticks open due to debris, carbon buildup, or age, manifold vacuum can bleed backward into the intake side of the booster. When you start the engine, the sudden rush of vacuum against a stuck valve collapses the diaphragm pressure, rendering the assist useless until the pedal is pumped enough to re-establish some differential pressure.

Another possibility involves the brake lights staying illuminated constantly when the engine is running. A constant load on the brake system can introduce heat and fluid expansion issues if the return spring isn't engaging properly, but more likely in this context, it indicates an electrical short that might be affecting the ABS module's ability to modulate pressure correctly during a diagnostic scan. However, since the ABS light is off, the module itself is likely not faulting out completely; rather, the system may be disabling assist features as a safety precaution due to sensor confusion regarding pedal position or pressure feedback.

To isolate this without tearing apart the dash, perform a vacuum test on the booster port with a gauge while the engine is idling. If the pressure drops significantly below the expected 18-20 inches of mercury (inHg), the booster diaphragm or check valve is failing. Alternatively, disconnecting the large vacuum hose from the booster and pressing the pedal should result in immediate firmness if the booster is at fault; if it remains soft even without engine vacuum, then a hidden leak downstream exists that isn't visible to the naked eye.

Given the vehicle's age and the recent replacement of various ignition and vacuum components, fatigue failure in the booster diaphragm or a seized check valve represents the highest probability for this specific symptom set. Addressing the electrical aspect by checking for shorts causing the brake lights to stay on is also advisable, as some modern ABS modules will inhibit hydraulic assist if they detect an invalid circuit state, even without illuminating the dashboard warning lamp immediately.
